en.title: Space exploration
en.summary: From Sputnik to the Moon, the space station and the telescope.

paragraphs: Space exploration is a story of competition and then cooperation. This lesson follows it from 1957 to today and trains you to speculate about the future, with the future continuous and past hypotheses.

The space age began in 1957, when the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite. On 20 July 1969 the American astronaut Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon, and he described the moment as one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind. Helen Sharman became the first Briton in space in 1991, and Tim Peake spent six months aboard the International Space Station in 2015 and 2016. The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, and the James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, have shown galaxies formed shortly after the beginning of the universe. Had the Apollo programme not been cancelled in 1972, humans might have reached Mars decades ago; some experts now expect that astronauts will be returning to the Moon by the end of this decade.

paragraphs: **1. Inverted conditionals for past hypotheses.** Had + subject + participle replaces if + past perfect. See Introduction to Grammar: Moods, command, subjunctive and conditional.

StandardInverted
If the programme had continued, humans might have reached Mars.Had the programme continued, humans might have reached Mars.

paragraphs: **2. Future continuous and speculation.** See Introduction to Grammar: Future and other tenses.

FormExample
will be + -ingAstronauts will be returning to the Moon.

items: **Launch** a rocket; **land** on the Moon; **orbit** the Earth.
**Astronaut** is used in the US and Europe; the Russian term is **cosmonaut**.
**Telescope** observes the sky; **satellite** circles the Earth.

paragraphs: Armstrong's words were carried by radio to an audience estimated at 600 million people, about one-fifth of the world's population at the time.
